note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: Three stages want a buffer at the same moment. The guard that holds a buffer borrows the whole pool exclusively, so a second guard is refused: two exclusive borrows of one thing.
In the pull request, someone wrapped the pool in a shared pointer and a mutex, and the error went away.
The compiler went quiet. Was that what it was asking for? Keep that question open, because the rest of the topic answers it, and rebuilds the pipeline with no locks at all.
See how the reflex happens, one real error at a time. Each patch fixes the message in front of you.
Two exclusive loans: so give each stage a thread. Now the closure may outlive the pool: so add move. Now the pool has moved into the first thread: so wrap it for sharing.
Sharing gives no mutable access: so add a mutex. Four errors, four patches.
Look back over them. Every patch was local, and none of them asked the question that matters: who should own the pool?
Count the cost of the design that was merged. One message passes through three stages.
Fill takes a buffer and counts it, inspect counts it, consume counts it and hands the buffer back.
How many times does a single message take a lock?
answer: Getting a buffer and putting it back each lock the pool, and each of the three stages locks the shared counters once.

A thousand messages make five thousand locks, and every one is a point where the stages must take turns. A later chapter measures that cost. For now, notice the question we have not asked yet: who owns the pool?

lines: Count the owners. The pool has three, main, fill and consume. The counters have four.
Every holder can call anything, any time. None is in charge.
So the invariant, every buffer is in the pool or in exactly one stage, lives in no single place.
Two locks in different orders can deadlock.
And how many buffers exist? Nothing here decides.
A mutex is an exclusive loan, checked while the program runs.
It owns its data and hands out mutable access through a guard. A second caller waits.
Hold a mutable borrow of it, and no one can lock it: no locking needed.
Use a lock, but only when nobody can be named as the single owner.
An arc clone copies a pointer. Zero allocations.
Now name the owner.
When the stages run in turn, one driver owns the pool, and each stage owns its own counters.
Loans go down: exclusive to fill, shared to inspect. The buffer is handed to consume and back. Results come up as plain values.
A thousand messages, one allocation, no locks.
If the stages must overlap, a tree isn't enough.
Be careful with the word shared. Four things in this pipeline get called that: the pool, the per stage counters, a read only configuration, and one buffer.
Which of them really has many owners at once?
answer: Eight threads read it for the whole run, and a spawned thread may outlive whoever would lend it, so it needs shared ownership. And since nobody writes it, it needs no mutex.
Everything else has exactly one owner at any moment: the driver, each stage in turn, or whoever holds the buffer. The rest only looked shared.

lines: Pipelines are graphs, and this one is a cycle.
A tree can't own a cycle. Try it with Rc pointers.
Drop your handles and every count falls to one, never zero. The ring keeps itself alive.
Four allocations, still live. The compiler won't stop a leak.
Here, we change who owns.
Give every node one owner: an arena, a vector of slots.
Edges become handles, an index plus a generation, eight bytes, cheap to copy.
So the cycle is just data. No node owns another.
Drop the arena and everything goes at once: zero live allocations, against four for the ring.
What the generation is for, next.
Here's why the generation matters.
The inspect stage, at index two, is hot-swapped. It's removed, and a new stage called audit takes the freed slot.
The fill stage still holds the old handle, with slot number two and generation zero.
So, what does looking up the old handle return?
answer: Removing inspect bumped the slot's generation to one. The old handle still says zero, so the lookup refuses.
A plain index would have quietly handed you the audit node. The wrong one.

lines: Slow motion, one slot's life.
Removal is three steps. Take the value out. Bump the generation, so older handles go stale. Put the index on the free list.
The next insert reuses the slot under the new generation.
A lookup checks both numbers. The new handle passes. The old one gets none.
One compare per access.
Sending is moving.
The sending half of a channel takes the buffer by value, like any other call.
The small part, id, pointer, capacity and length, crosses over. The big buffer stays.
Using the sender's variable afterwards is the use-after-move error.
Cloning would copy a second buffer, every message. Copy the id out first.
Now a move closure.
A closure captures what it uses as lightly as it can. This one only needs a mutable borrow of the pool.
But a thread may outlive its function, so the borrow is refused: the closure-may-outlive error.
Move makes the closure own the pool. The thread owns it until it ends, and join hands it back.
Now the stages run at once.
One thread owns the pool and alone makes buffers: three, one per stage.
Each stage receives a buffer, works on it, and sends it on. The last sends it home.
At every instant, each buffer has exactly one owner: a stage, the owner, or a channel.
A thousand messages, three buffers, no locks.
Now break it.
Stage three stalls, in the pull request, and in the ring.
How many buffers exist in each, by the time stage three wakes?
answer: A thousand in the pull request. Three in the ring.
In the pull request, stage one makes its own buffers, and its channel never pushes back.
In the ring, only the owner makes buffers. The first stage just waits for a buffer to come home. The waiting comes from the shape of the program, not from a setting.

lines: One owner means one set of books, and that is a real advantage, not a slogan.
Every channel is first in, first out and every buffer takes the same route, so the owner always knows which buffer must come home next.
If a buffer were cloned or lost, the check fails immediately. We tried both, and both were caught.
And while the check passes the books balance, at every one of a thousand returns: buffers in the pool plus buffers out in the ring equal every buffer ever made.
So how do you choose? Look at the shape of the data, and not at the error message.
A natural parent: a tree, and no locks at all. A graph with cycles or removal: an arena.
Many concurrent users of one piece of state: an owner thread.
Small simple data touched briefly: a mutex is fine.
First ask: who should own this?
The mutex is not the villain, so do not over learn the lesson. Using it to silence the compiler is the mistake, not the tool.
The async runtime's own guide puts a map of simple values behind a mutex, keeps each critical section short, and moves state into a task that owns it once the work needs input and output.
Read only data shared for the whole run needs only the shared pointer, with no lock.
If a lock does become contended, the fixes are an owner task, splitting the data, or restructuring to avoid it. Measuring that is chapter four, and the thread safety rules are chapter six.
Prove it. One of three.
One stage borrows a view of the first five bytes of its buffer. Next, it sends the whole buffer onward. Afterwards, it prints that view.
What does the compiler say?
answer: The buffer cannot leave. The view still points into it. Another thread could change those bytes.
Take the header as a value first. Then send.

lines: Prove it. Two of three.
In the ring, stage three stalls. Point to the exact line where stage one blocks.
answer: The first stage only works on a buffer that is sent to it. With the third stage stalled, none come back. Nothing it sends ever blocks.

lines: Prove it. Three of three.
A job scheduler on one thread. Jobs depend on jobs, and a finished job is removed while others still list it.
Which ownership shape?
answer: One owner for every job, handles for the dependencies, and a finished job answers none.

lines: Four shapes for one pipeline.
An arc of mutex: many owners and a lock, hiding who should own the data.
A tree: one owner lends down. An arena: handles as edges.
An owner thread: sent owned values, one owner per buffer.
Every topology still lends: fill borrows exclusively, inspect shared.
Next: many shared borrows, or one exclusive borrow, never both.
